mappings.note: Ordering four invertebrate phyla by body complexity is LO-5's ladder run end to end -- cellular, tissue, organ, organ system -- with each rung naming its phylum. The word 'evolutionary' in the stem is decoration: the ordering is done purely on levels of organisation, so not C4.5.

The Rigveda and Brihat Samhita classifying animals by habitat and ecological role: C6.1 for India's contribution to the matter being studied, C5.1 because the source is literature and the item is about literature having done science. Not C4.2-LO-9, which covers the European succession of kingdom systems.

Amphioxus shows a notochord at some stage of life, which is the criterion that admits an animal to the chordates -- LO-5's use of body organisation to place an animal. Chordata and protochordates have no outcome of their own in this curriculum.

Why angiosperms became the dominant plant group: flowers raising pollination efficiency and fruits protecting and dispersing seeds. That is adaptive structure and function, C4.5, not C4.2 -- no level of body organisation is traced, and the reproductive apparatus the item rests on has no outcome at all.

Picks the one unicellular member of a mostly multicellular kingdom -- C-4.1-LO-1's 'number of cells present', used within a kingdom rather than to reach one. Not C-4.1-LO-2: Fungi is given, nothing is placed.

Thallophyta identified by an undifferentiated thallus with no true root, stem or leaf -- body organisation, the C4.2 competency where the plant divisions sit. Not C-4.1-LO-1: cell number and nutrition play no part; the discriminator is differentiation of the body.

Mammary glands as the change that raises offspring survival -- C4.5's 'structure, and function of organisms'. Not C4.2-LO-5: Mammalia is a class inside an already-placed phylum, and no level of organisation is being traced.

Applies the naming rule to a newly found animal: shared genus with tiger and lion means the first word must be Panthera. LO-4 (apply) rather than LO-3 (state the rules), because the item hands over a real organism to name.

Unicellular plus true nucleus, with mixed nutrition, resolved to Protista -- placement into a kingdom, C-4.1-LO-2. The features come from the figure, so the work is the assignment, not the observation.

The ask is the cell wall constituent, chitin -- a structural characteristic, C-4.1-LO-1. The decomposer role in the stem is only framing; contrast the four-organism table item, where the decomposer role was the actual answer and so took C-4.1-LO-2.

Fern stem section showing conducting tissue, set against mosses -- the plant-division family's body-organisation half, C4.2. Same reading as the other fern-against-moss items; this curriculum offers no plant outcome to separate them with.

Repeating segments plus a body cavity giving flexibility and fine control of movement -- LO-7 verbatim, 'explains what a body built of repeating segments makes possible'. Not C4.2-LO-5: Annelida has its own row and this item is precisely what it describes.

POOR FIT, fourth of the rank-hierarchy items: Kingdom at the broad end, Species at the narrow end where members interbreed. No outcome in curriculum 82 covers taxonomic ranks, so C-4.1-LO-2 is cited for its 'classify organisms in groups' clause only.
Bare definition of an endemic species as one restricted to a region -- distribution of life, C2.8. No conservation judgement is asked, which is what keeps it off C5.2 where the hotspot items sit.

Two Indian endemics named. Same home as the definition item: this is where organisms occur, not what should be done about them. Not C6.1 -- India appears here as a place on the map, not as a contributor to science.

The significance of hotspots is stated as their crucial role in conservation, which is C5.2's named example. The split used throughout: endemism as distribution goes to C2.8, hotspots as a conservation priority to C5.2.

Defines classification itself as grouping organisms by similarities and differences -- the opening verb of C-4.1-LO-2. A generic definition with no kingdom, rank or criterion attached, so the outcome's own basis clause does not apply; nothing closer exists.

Small differences aiding adaptation and accumulating over generations -- natural selection and its consequences, C4.5. Not C2.8: the answer is about how new forms arise, not about the systems that support them.
Names two broad criteria, cell structure and mode of nutrition, which are two of the three C-4.1-LO-1 lists. The purest statement of that outcome in the chapter.

Why the two-kingdom system created confusion -- LO-9 opens with 'Explains why the two-kingdom system was set aside', so this is the outcome's own wording. Not C-4.1-LO-2, which uses the surviving system rather than criticising the old one.

Who proposed the five kingdoms and when. Recall at the shallow end of LO-9's 'move to a five-kingdom classification'; it shares that row with the chronology and match-the-scientist items because the succession of systems has exactly one home here.

One distinguishing characteristic of Monera, single-celled and lacking a true nucleus -- cell number and cellular organisation, C-4.1-LO-1. Not C-4.1-LO-2: the kingdom is given and the item asks what marks it, not where an organism belongs.

Cell wall composition in protists (cellulose) -- a cellular-organisation characteristic, C-4.1-LO-1. Paired deliberately against the fungal chitin item, which sits on the same row for the same reason.

Protists as oxygen producers and as food for small animals -- the 'ecological role organisms play' clause that C-4.1-LO-2 adds to C-4.1-LO-1. Not LO-15: a role in a food chain is named, but no interaction between two named groups is analysed.

Fungi as decomposers returning minerals to the soil -- again the ecological-role clause of C-4.1-LO-2, and the same row as the protist-role item. The two share it honestly: this curriculum has one outcome covering what a kingdom does in an ecosystem.
